writing.exampleCaption: Same request, three different blocking stories underneath.
writing.explanation:
HTTP/1.1 can reuse connections, but response ordering and limited pipelining often led browsers to open multiple connections. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, which removes application-level blocking but not TCP's — one lost packet still stalls every stream. HTTP/3 moves onto QUIC over UDP, so loss recovery can proceed independently per affected stream; congestion control still applies to the connection. Its handshake integrates TLS.

HTTP/1.1 can reuse connections, but responses on a connection are generally constrained by request ordering in common deployments. Pipelining exists in the protocol but saw limited browser use; clients often opened several connections to avoid waiting behind one slow response. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection and compresses headers, improving concurrent request handling. Because all streams still share that TCP connection, packet loss can cause transport-level head-of-line blocking even when the HTTP streams are logically separate.

HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which uses UDP and implements independent streams and integrated TLS. Loss of data for one QUIC stream need not hold back application data on unaffected streams in the same way as TCP's ordered byte stream. A lost packet may carry frames for several streams, and congestion control can slow the whole connection. It does not make the network loss disappear, and congestion control still affects the whole connection. Connection setup, migration, proxies, and server support also matter in practice. Version numbers do not tell you whether a specific page will be faster without measuring its request pattern and network conditions.

For an interview, draw two requests where one response stalls. Explain which layer causes the delay in each version. Then mention compatibility and observability: TLS negotiation, middleboxes, fallback, and server configuration may determine what a client actually uses. Avoid a universal 'six connections' claim; browsers and workloads vary. The clean answer is about where multiplexing lives and which ordering constraint remains.

A page load can mix versions because the browser negotiates each connection with its origin and intermediaries. Inspect the actual protocol in developer tools before attributing a measured improvement to HTTP/3. A CDN, proxy, or server configuration can dominate the result even when the browser supports the newer protocol.
writing.feedback: TCP must deliver in order, so the whole connection waits.
